Hsing and James Moyer, initially targeting notebook computer power rails with highly integrated, high-frequency monolithic power ICs. First, the BOM displacement narrative: by integrating bipolar, CMOS, and DMOS processes into a proprietary BCD platform, MPS designs power modules that collapse discrete component bills of materials, enabling customers to source a single integrated solution rather than many chips from multiple vendors. This drives deeper socket wins, higher average selling prices, and stickier design relationships. chapters.title: The Power Architect: MPS at the Epicenter of AI Infrastructure and Automotive Electrification
chapters.body:
## The Current Moment

When Monolithic Power Systems reported first-quarter 2026 results in late April, the numbers carried a charge that few analog semiconductor companies have generated in recent memory. Revenue reached $804.2 million, a 26.1 percent increase year-over-year, beating the Wall Street consensus of roughly $781.6 million by more than $22 million. Non-GAAP earnings per share of $5.10 cleared the $4.90 estimate. Then management guided second-quarter revenue of $890 million to $910 million — a sequential increase of approximately 12 percent that, if achieved, would place Monolithic Power Systems on a full-year revenue trajectory approaching $3.5 billion, up from $2.79 billion in fiscal 2025. The catalyst was not a product cycle surprise. It was the deepening entrenchment of MPS power-delivery silicon inside NVIDIA's GPU roadmap, with analyst estimates placing MPS content at approximately 70 percent of addressable power management silicon per Vera Rubin GPU tray — a franchise position that had transformed a niche fabless analog designer into one of the most consequential infrastructure suppliers in the artificial intelligence supply chain.

## Three Pillars, One Platform

The MPS investment thesis rests on three interlocking structural positions, each reinforced by the same underlying asset: a proprietary bipolar-CMOS-DMOS (BCD) process platform that competitors cannot easily replicate.

The first pillar is AI data center power delivery. Enterprise Data segment revenue grew from approximately $148 million in fiscal 2023 to roughly $702 million in fiscal 2025 — a compound rate exceeding 100 percent over two years. Management guided a floor of 50 percent growth for fiscal 2026, implying more than $1 billion from that segment alone. MPS's multi-phase digital controllers, including the MP2891 dual-loop eight-phase controller, and its integrated MPM-series power modules address the escalating demands of GPU trays already exceeding 1,000 watts per socket under the Blackwell architecture. Design wins in NVIDIA reference platforms are inherently sticky: once a power architecture is qualified into a generation's reference design, it propagates across tens of millions of units and is locked in for the product cycle.

The second pillar is automotive electrification and ADAS proliferation. Automotive became MPS's second-largest end market in fiscal 2025, generating $592.5 million in revenue — a 43 percent increase year-over-year — as both Western and Chinese OEM supply chains adopted MPS motor drivers, battery management ICs, exterior lighting drivers, and domain-controller power rails. The growth was not purely an EV story: internal combustion and hybrid platforms adopting 48-volt mild-hybrid architectures, expanding ADAS radar and camera subsystems, and the transition from hub-and-spoke wiring harnesses to domain-controller vehicle architectures all expanded MPS's addressable content per vehicle independently of battery electric penetration rates.

The third pillar is BOM displacement through BCD-integrated modules. MPS's MPM-series power modules collapse multi-chip discrete power architectures — controller, field-effect transistors, inductors, decoupling capacitors — into a single standardized package. This reduces engineer design time, cuts component counts, and improves thermal management in dense boards. The strategy mirrors approaches at Analog Devices and Texas Instruments but is executed with a higher degree of proprietary integration. The consequence is structurally higher average selling prices, deeper customer relationships, and a pricing dynamic insulated from the commodity erosion that afflicts standalone IC suppliers.

## The Financial Foundation

Fiscal 2025 established the financial baseline from which the forward narrative unfolds. Revenue of $2.79 billion grew 26.4 percent year-over-year, with GAAP gross margin of 55.2 percent — a level sustained across all four quarters and reflective of BCD process advantage, rising module mix, and AI infrastructure pricing power. GAAP operating income of $729 million carried a 26.1 percent operating margin; non-GAAP operating margins exceeded 35 percent throughout the year, with Q1 2026's GAAP operating margin of 30.0 percent signaling that operating leverage was beginning to assert itself as enterprise data revenue scaled. Normalized GAAP net income was $621 million, with diluted earnings per share of $12.86.

The balance sheet is structurally differentiated from most high-growth semiconductor peers. Stockholders' equity of $3.53 billion includes $2.61 billion in retained earnings; total liabilities stand at only $662.7 million; long-term debt is zero. In February 2026, the board raised the quarterly cash dividend 28 percent to $2.00 per share — an unusual signal of free-cash-flow confidence from a company growing revenue at 26 percent annually.

| Metric | FY2021 | FY2023 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue ($M) | 1,208 | 1,821 | 2,790 |
| Gross Margin | — | 56.1% | 55.2% |
| Operating Income ($M) | 262 | 482 | 729 |
| Net Income ($M) | 242 | 427 | 621 |
| Long-Term Debt | $0 | $0 | $0 |

## The Valuation Tension

At a market capitalization of approximately $79 billion as of late May 2026, and a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of approximately 120, Monolithic Power Systems is not priced as an analog semiconductor company. Texas Instruments, the sector's largest player by revenue at approximately $17 billion, trades at roughly 25 times earnings. Analog Devices trades at approximately 30 times. MPS is priced as a high-growth compounder whose near-term revenue trajectory — driven by AI infrastructure design wins and automotive electrification content expansion — justifies a multiple more commonly associated with software platforms than with fabless silicon suppliers dependent on foundry capacity, customer capital expenditure cycles, and competitive design-in processes.

That tension — between MPS's formidable operational record and the demands the current valuation places on its future execution — is the animating question of this dossier. The chapters that follow examine how durable the AI data center revenue franchise actually is beyond the Vera Rubin generation; whether automotive can sustain 40-plus percent annual growth as electrification timelines extend and Chinese OEM competition intensifies; and whether the premium multiple attached to MPWR shares can be justified on a credible earnings path through 2030. The answers will determine whether Michael Hsing's twenty-eight-year integration play has permanently altered MPS's standing in the analog semiconductor hierarchy, or whether the current moment represents a peak concentration of favorable variables unlikely to persist.

chapters.title: Founding Vision to S&P 500: The Twenty-Eight-Year Arc of Michael Hsing's Power Integration Thesis
chapters.body:
## The Power Problem That Founded a Company

When Michael R. Hsing incorporated Monolithic Power Systems on August 22, 1997 in San Jose, California, the notebook computer had become the fastest-growing segment in personal computing — and its power architecture was a mess. The prevailing design relied on discrete assemblies of MOSFETs, inductors, and linear regulators sourced from multiple vendors, occupying precious board real estate and dissipating energy as heat with inefficiencies that shortened battery life and complicated thermal design for OEM engineers. Linear regulators, then ubiquitous in portable devices, achieved regulation by burning excess voltage as heat — elegant in concept, ruinous at scale.

Hsing, who had spent years developing high-voltage silicon process technology at Micrel Semiconductor and Supertex Inc., believed the solution was structural rather than incremental. His thesis was that a proprietary BCD process — integrating bipolar, CMOS, and DMOS transistor families on a single die — could collapse those multi-chip discrete architectures into a compact monolithic switching regulator operating at higher frequencies than competitors thought practical. Higher frequency meant smaller passive components, smaller total footprint, and efficiency curves that linear regulators could not approach. He recruited co-founder James Moyer, who brought complementary circuit design expertise, and the two began assembling a small team of power-analog engineers in San Jose with that single conviction: monolithic integration would eventually win every power rail it entered.

The competitive risk in 1997 was not abstract. The dominant suppliers to notebook OEMs — International Rectifier, Maxim Integrated, Linear Technology — had established qualification relationships and multi-year design-in cycles that made displacement slow and uncertain. MPS had no revenue, no established foundry relationship, and a product thesis that required customers to trust an unproven process at frequencies that many board designers considered unreliable. The company self-funded through early design wins in notebook voltage regulation and LCD backlight driving, using those revenues to fund successive process generations rather than returning capital to investors.

## The IPO Window and the Consumer Electronics Bet

By 2004, the MPS product catalog had achieved sufficient breadth across notebook power management and LCD driver ICs to support a public offering. The company listed on NASDAQ under the ticker MPWR in November 2004, raising capital that funded expanded headcount and a second R&D center in Chengdu, China — a decision that would prove to be among the most consequential in MPS's infrastructure history. The Chengdu facility, now the company's largest R&D site globally with more than 2,800 engineers in the China region, was established at a moment when few fabless semiconductor firms were making long-term commitments to build engineering depth rather than simply sourcing lower-cost labor in mainland China.

The post-IPO years through 2010 extended the BCD platform into consumer electronics broadly — gaming controllers, flat-panel television power stages, digital cameras, and set-top box power management. Revenue diversified beyond notebook OEM concentration, and the company developed the cadence of frequent product introductions that would later characterize its catalog expansion. The period was not without margin pressure: consumer electronics commanded lower ASPs and proved more cyclical than MPS's early notebook segment. But it built the process yield data and design reuse libraries that made later industrial and automotive qualifications possible.

## The First Non-Obvious Bet: Digital Control for Server Power Rails

The period between 2010 and 2018 represented the most consequential strategic repositioning in MPS's history — one that was far from obvious at execution time. As cloud computing buildout accelerated server rack density through the early 2010s, the power delivery requirements for enterprise CPUs and, later, GPUs demanded a new controller architecture. The analog pulse-width modulation controllers that had served notebook and consumer designs well were increasingly inadequate for the tight voltage tolerances and transient response requirements of data center processors operating at sub-one-volt rails with current draws exceeding 100 amperes.

MPS invested in digital multi-phase controller development — implementing programmable control loops, telemetry interfaces, and PMBus communication in silicon — at a time when the market for such products was nascent and Intersil, Renesas, and International Rectifier held incumbent positions. The competitive risk was real: digital controllers required OEM engineers to adopt new configuration workflows, and the incumbent suppliers were deeply embedded with server motherboard design teams. MPS's approach offered tighter load regulation and faster fault response, but winning initial design-ins required displacing engineers' habits as much as their vendors.

The bet paid out slowly, then rapidly. By the 2018–2022 period, MPS's multi-phase digital controller family had accumulated sufficient design wins in enterprise motherboards and communications line cards to be treated as a genuine alternative to the incumbent field. The enterprise data segment — then called "computing and storage" in MPS's segment reporting — began its ascent from what management described internally as a seed investment into a second strategic pillar.

## Automotive Certification and the Long Qualification Runway

The second non-obvious bet was the early commitment to automotive-grade IC qualification programs. The automotive semiconductor market operates on qualification timelines measured in years and qualification standards — AEC-Q100 for ICs, ISO 26262 for functional safety — that require separate design, testing, and documentation infrastructure from consumer and industrial product lines. MPS established its Munich, Germany design center and began building automotive-specific design flows around 2012–2014, at a point when the revenue opportunity from motor drivers and LED drivers for conventional internal combustion vehicles was modest and the electrification thesis was speculative.

The investment logic was that the qualification runway itself was the barrier to entry. By beginning AEC-Q100 processes early, MPS would have automotive-qualified ICs ready to insert into new vehicle platform programs that took three to five years from design win to production. Competitors who entered automotive later would face the same multi-year qualification delay. The automotive segment generated $592.5 million in FY2025 revenue, growing 43 percent year-over-year — a result that required groundwork laid a decade earlier.

## Module Platform and S&P 500 Inclusion

The third inflection was the MPM-series power module strategy, which MPS launched in earnest around 2018–2019. Where conventional IC suppliers sold controllers and FETs as discrete components that OEM engineers assembled with passives onto printed circuit boards, the MPM platform bundled controller, integrated FETs, inductors, and decoupling capacitors into a single standardized package. The pitch to engineering teams was reduced design time and shorter time-to-market; the strategic logic for MPS was higher ASPs, stickier customer relationships, and insulation from the commodity pricing dynamics of standalone ICs.

The module strategy positioned MPS as a "solution company" — a framing Hsing used repeatedly in earnings calls during this period — rather than a component supplier. The transition carried execution risk: module customers needed to trust that MPS's integrated thermal management and passive selection would meet their reliability requirements across environmental extremes, a more demanding qualification bar than a bare IC. But as the enterprise data and automotive segments scaled, the module approach became a competitive differentiator against Texas Instruments and Analog Devices, who pursued parallel strategies with longer lead times on new form factors.

MPS's inclusion in the S&P 500 in February 2021 marked the structural market milestone that formalized the company's transition from a specialized mid-cap analog designer into an institutional-grade equity. The index addition mechanically required passive funds to acquire MPWR shares and shifted the company's shareholder base toward large institutional holders — a change in governance dynamics, investor relations expectations, and analyst coverage depth that accompanied MPS's emergence as a franchise semiconductor company rather than a specialty niche designer.

## IP Defense as Competitive Infrastructure

Running through each phase of MPS's history is a thread of intellectual property litigation that reflects the nature of competing with proprietary process technology in a landscape of well-capitalized incumbents. The April 30, 2026 victory in the Bel Power Solutions case — in which the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas granted MPS summary judgment of non-infringement on all six asserted semiconductor patent claims and ordered Bel Power to pay $50,000 in court costs — was the most recent chapter in that posture. For a fabless firm whose competitive advantage is embedded in process recipes and circuit topologies rather than physical manufacturing assets, the willingness to defend IP aggressively is itself a strategic signal to potential entrants.

By the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, the twenty-eight-year arc from Hsing and Moyer's 1997 founding thesis had produced an enterprise with more than $2.79 billion in FY2025 revenue, a catalog exceeding 4,000 products across thirteen product lines, and a position at the critical path of GPU power delivery for AI infrastructure — an outcome that required, at each inflection, a willingness to make long-duration investments whose payoffs were measured in product cycles rather than quarters.

chapters.title: The BCD Advantage: Product Families, Platform Integration, and the Shift from Silicon to Systems
chapters.body:
## The Process Foundation: Why BCD Cannot Be Commoditized

The semiconductor industry's most durable moats are not built from software or brand recognition — they are etched, layer by layer, into proprietary process technology that takes decades and hundreds of millions of dollars to replicate. Monolithic Power Systems' core competitive asset was the BCD platform: a co-integrated stack of bipolar, CMOS, and DMOS transistor families sharing a single silicon die. Each element served a distinct functional role. Bipolar devices delivered the precision, low-noise amplification required for analog control loops and reference voltage generation. CMOS logic enabled low-power digital circuitry — PMBus interface stacks, telemetry engines, protection logic — without materially raising leakage or die area. DMOS, the double-diffused metal-oxide-semiconductor layer, provided the high-voltage, high-current switching transistors capable of handling the power rails that commodity CMOS would destroy.

The integration challenge was non-trivial. Commodity CMOS foundries optimize thermal budgets, implant energies, and oxide thicknesses for one objective: density of logic transistors at minimum pitch. Introducing high-voltage DMOS devices on the same substrate required different implant profiles, deeper junctions, and modified isolation structures that conflicted with advanced logic scaling. Standard pure-play foundries running TSMC N5 or Samsung GAA nodes could not simply add DMOS capability; the process modifications would degrade logic density and violate the economics of their baseline node. MPS's BCD process, developed over nearly three decades of in-house iteration, encoded this integration in its design rules, SPICE models, and design-kit libraries — intellectual property that was practically irreproducible on a commodity CMOS roadmap.

The MP2891 dual-loop 8-phase VR14 digital controller illustrated what that process advantage produced in product form. A VR14-compliant controller managing eight synchronous buck converter phases simultaneously — tracking CPU or GPU load transients in microseconds, balancing current across phases to within fractions of an ampere, reporting power telemetry to the host over PMBus, and protecting against over-temperature and over-current faults — required high-voltage gate-drive capability, precision analog current sensing, and a digital control engine on the same die. Separating those functions across multiple chips was possible; integrating them on a single BCD die was what allowed MPS to shrink the power delivery circuit to a fraction of the board area its discrete competitors required, and what drove the design wins that anchored the enterprise data segment's acceleration from $148 million in FY2023 to approximately $702 million in FY2025.

## A Taxonomy of Power: Six Product Families

MPS organized its more than 4,000 products into six segment-aligned families by the mid-2020s.

The **storage and computing family** — DC/DC buck converters, multi-phase digital controllers, and integrated power stages for CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, and memory — was the highest-ASP, highest-volume cluster, generating $732.5 million in FY2025. The MP2891 sat at the apex; below it, the MP2856 and related multi-phase families served mainstream notebook, server, and discrete GPU voltage regulation across AMD, Intel, and NVIDIA reference platforms.

The **automotive family** covered motor drivers for HVAC blowers, window regulators, fuel pumps, and mirror actuators; LED drivers for exterior lighting (headlamps, DRLs, taillights); battery management and charging ICs for 12V and 48V architectures; and 48V-to-12V DC/DC converters for mild-hybrid zone controllers. The MP54XX series multi-phase buck converters handled ADAS radar and camera power rails. Automotive generated $592.5 million in FY2025, a 43% year-over-year increase, spanning both combustion-platform 48V adoption and EV-platform domain controllers.

The **enterprise data family** — distinct from storage and computing — comprised the VR14-compliant controllers and MPM-series integrated modules for GPU accelerator trays, switch-silicon power rails, and hyperscaler memory subsystems. This was the fastest-growing segment, with revenue compounding at over 100% in the two years ending December 2025.

The **communications family** supplied line-card DC/DC converters, optical module power managers, and base-station power ICs for Cisco, Ericsson, Nokia, and the Huawei/ZTE ecosystem. Revenue was approximately $309 million in FY2025. The **consumer and mobile family** — smartphone fast-charger controllers, battery fuel gauges, display backlighting drivers, gaming console power modules — was MPS's legacy entry market and remained margin-dilutive relative to enterprise and automotive. The **industrial and medical family** produced motor drivers for robotics and factory automation, isolated DC/DC converters for medical instrumentation, and AC/DC controllers for industrial power supplies, generating approximately $199 million in FY2025.

## The Module Imperative: BOM Displacement as Business Model

A standalone IC was a component; a power module was a solution. MPS's MPM-series integrated power modules embedded the DC/DC controller, synchronous MOSFET switches, bootstrap diode, output inductor, and bulk decoupling capacitors within a single shielded package — replacing three to seven discrete components on a customer's bill of materials with one line item. The distinction mattered structurally. A customer adopting a standalone IC still required a power supply engineer to select external FETs, size the inductor, manage thermal performance, and qualify each passive component supplier. A customer adopting an MPM module purchased a pre-qualified, thermally characterized system that could be dropped into a reference design with minimal engineering intervention.

The pricing premium reflected that engineering value transfer. While standalone multi-phase controller ICs for enterprise server applications sold in volume for several dollars per unit, fully integrated power modules for the same rail — handling 30 to 100 amperes in a single package — commanded ASPs an order of magnitude higher, with analyst estimates of module ASPs in the range of $15 to $50 for high-current AI server applications versus $3 to $8 for comparable standalone controllers and drivers purchased separately. The BOM reduction for a hyperscaler OEM adopting a module architecture versus discrete components was estimated at 40 to 60 percent fewer passive components per power rail, with corresponding PCB area savings of 30 to 50 percent in dense GPU tray designs — a compelling total-cost argument that extended beyond the silicon sticker price.

The April 2026 patent ruling in MPS's favor against Bel Power Solutions reinforced freedom-to-operate across this module architecture and validated the legal defensibility of MPS's integrated package designs. The ruling cleared a potential royalty overhang on the company's highest-margin product category at a strategically important moment in the enterprise data ramp.

## Wide-Bandgap: The Gate Driver Adjacency

Silicon carbide and gallium nitride power devices required fundamentally different gate-drive conditions than silicon IGBTs or MOSFETs — faster edge rates, tighter timing control, isolated high-side drive, and active protection against false turn-on from high dV/dt transients. MPS's gate driver product line for SiC and GaN addressed the EV traction inverter, industrial motor drive, and fast-charger markets, where wide-bandgap devices were rapidly displacing silicon in high-efficiency, high-frequency applications.

The strategic rationale was straightforward: automotive OEMs and their Tier 1 inverter suppliers — Continental, Bosch, Denso — were transitioning production EV drivetrains to SiC MOSFETs for their superior switching characteristics at 400V and 800V bus architectures. MPS's gate driver ICs sat directly in that signal path. The competitive landscape in this specific niche was crowded: Wolfspeed supplied SiC substrates and packaged devices directly and qualified companion gate drivers; Infineon offered the EiceDriver family with extensive SiC/GaN support; STMicroelectronics competed across both SiC power devices and the gate driver layer. MPS's differentiation was integration — pairing gate drive with protection, isolation, and current sensing in a BCD-enabled single-die solution rather than a two-chip approach — but the company had not yet established the automotive design-win density in wide-bandgap gate drive that it had achieved in conventional voltage regulation.

## Enterprise Data and the Qualification Clock

Qualification in the GPU power delivery context was a multi-stage process that compressed roughly 12 to 18 months from initial silicon submission to meaningful revenue contribution. MPS engineering teams worked directly with NVIDIA's platform architects during reference design validation — characterizing transient response, thermal performance under sustained load, and PMBus telemetry accuracy against VR14 specification tolerances. Passing platform-level qualification locked the device into the NVIDIA reference design bill of materials, which then propagated across every ODM — Foxconn, Quanta, Wistron, Inventec — building to that platform. The stickiness was structural: re-qualification of an alternative supplier mid-generation required NVIDIA to restart the validation sequence and accept design risk, creating a strong incumbent preference once initial qualification was achieved.

The MP2891's qualification into Blackwell-generation GPU platforms established the design methodology that MPS carried forward into the Vera Rubin architecture. Analyst estimates circulating in early 2026 suggested MPS content per Vera Rubin GPU tray at approximately 70 percent of addressable power management silicon — a step-function increase reflecting both deeper integration per rail and expansion into new power domains within the tray architecture. CFO Bernie Blegen revised the enterprise data growth floor for FY2026 upward to "at least 50%" on the Q4 2025 earnings call, citing improving backlog visibility and broadening customer diversification beyond the NVIDIA anchor.

## White Spaces and Contested Ground

MPS's product taxonomy, for all its breadth, left material ground to incumbents with deeper roots. Texas Instruments held entrenched positions in reference voltage, precision op-amps, data converters, and the broadest catalog of commodity DC/DC controllers — product categories where TI's manufacturing scale, distributor relationships, and design-in legacy created switching costs MPS had not yet meaningfully attacked. Analog Devices dominated in high-precision measurement, isolated interfaces, and the signal chain adjacent to power conversion in industrial and medical applications. Renesas occupied a structurally different position: its automotive MCU franchise created natural pull-through for co-integrated power management on the same chipset bill of materials, a bundled solution architecture MPS could not replicate without an MCU product line of its own.

In MPS's FY2025 10-K, management acknowledged the competitive landscape in terms of "established analog companies with broader product portfolios, greater financial resources, and deeper customer relationships in certain segments," without specifying which product lines represented the clearest displacement targets. Investor day presentations through 2025 emphasized continued expansion into industrial motor drive — a TI and ADI stronghold — and communications infrastructure power, where hyperscaler custom silicon designs were beginning to open new qualification cycles. The implicit strategy was not frontal assault on TI's catalog breadth, but continued BCD-enabled integration and module density where discrete competitors could not follow on process economics alone.

chapters.title: From $1.2 Billion to $2.8 Billion: Revenue Velocity, Margin Structure, and the Capital Allocation Framework
chapters.body:
----------|---------|------------|
| FY2021 | $1.208B | — |
| FY2022 | $1.794B | +48.5% |
| FY2023 | $1.821B | +1.5% |
| FY2024 | $2.207B | +21.2% |
| FY2025 | $2.790B | +26.4% |

The table conceals as much as it reveals. The FY2022 surge — nearly 49% — was genuine demand acceleration: pandemic-driven pull-forward across consumer electronics, notebooks, and server infrastructure collided with a supply environment still catching up from the 2020–2021 shortage. MPS, with its diversified customer base and stronger-than-average foundry relationships, captured outsized share during allocation constraints. The FY2022→FY2023 near-flat revenue — growth of just 1.5% on a base that had nearly doubled — was not a company-specific failure but the semiconductor industry's self-inflicted correction: customers who had double- and triple-ordered to secure supply began burning through bloated inventory rather than placing new orders, and channel demand normalized sharply. MPS's FY2023 performance, while disappointing relative to the prior year's trajectory, compared favorably to several analog peers that saw actual revenue declines. Texas Instruments reported a 12% revenue decline in FY2023; Analog Devices fell approximately 6%. That MPS held essentially flat — and maintained operating income above $480 million — reflected the early stages of enterprise data segment revenue that partially offset consumer and computing weakness. The inventory correction ran its course through mid-2024, and the FY2024 reacceleration to +21% preceded the AI-driven step-change that defined FY2025.

## The FY2025 Revenue Mix: Where Growth Actually Came From

The aggregate $2.79 billion figure for FY2025 masks a significant internal restructuring of the revenue base. Storage and Computing remained the largest segment at $732.5 million, representing 26% of total revenue, but its 46% growth rate was itself partly a function of enterprise SSD controller and memory module demand rather than traditional notebook power rails. Automotive, at $592.5 million and 21% of revenue, delivered 43% growth — a performance driven not solely by EV volume but by 48V mild-hybrid architecture adoption across European and Chinese platforms, expanding ADAS radar and camera power rail content, and domain-controller proliferation reducing per-vehicle wiring while increasing per-vehicle IC content.

| Segment | FY2025 Revenue | % of Total | YoY Growth |
|---------|----------------|------------|------------|
| Storage & Computing | $732.5M | 26% | +46% |
| Enterprise Data | ~$702M | 25% | >100% (cumulative +166% over 2 years) |
| Automotive | $592.5M | 21% | +43% |
| Communications | ~$309M | 11% | — |
| Consumer | ~$255M | 9% | — |
| Industrial | ~$199M | 7% | — |

Enterprise Data was the inflection point. The segment generated approximately $148 million in FY2023 and roughly $702 million in FY2025 — a cumulative expansion of approximately 166% in two years, representing one of the fastest organic revenue ramp rates in MPS's history and, arguably, in the analog semiconductor sector at large. The source of that growth was MPS's qualification into NVIDIA's Blackwell GPU reference architecture, supplying VR14-compliant multi-phase digital controllers and integrated power modules for high-density GPU server trays drawing in excess of 1,000 watts per socket. The segment's share of total revenue shifted from approximately 8% in FY2023 to roughly 25% in FY2025 — a mix shift that materially altered the company's margin profile and growth sustainability calculus.

## The Gross Margin Paradox: Scaling Without Diluting

The conventional expectation when a semiconductor company ramps a new, fast-growing segment — particularly one involving complex system-level modules rather than commodity ICs — is some gross margin dilution as learning curves are absorbed and initial production runs carry higher unit costs. MPS confounded that expectation through all four quarters of FY2025. GAAP gross margin held in the 55.1–55.4% range across every quarter, settling at 55.2% for the full year — effectively identical to the prior three years.

Three structural factors explain the stability. First, the enterprise data segment commands pricing power unavailable in consumer or industrial channels: power delivery into an NVIDIA GPU tray is mission-critical infrastructure, qualification cycles are long and expensive, and switching costs are high. MPS has been able to price accordingly. Second, the shift toward MPM-series integrated power modules — packaging controller, FETs, inductors, and passives into a single qualified unit — carries structurally higher ASPs than standalone controller ICs. Modules are not simply higher-revenue-per-unit; they are meaningfully higher-margin because the integration value commands a premium that exceeds the incremental assembly and component cost. Third, the foundry pricing environment through 2024 and 2025 was stable. MPS's proprietary BCD process runs primarily on mature nodes at foundries in Taiwan and China; absent the leading-edge node capacity constraints that afflict logic chipmakers, the foundry cost per wafer did not escalate materially.

Q2 2026 guidance of 55.1–55.7% gross margin suggests this stability persists into at least the first half of next year. The risks to compression are identifiable but not imminent: commoditization of VR controller designs if NVIDIA's power delivery architecture becomes more standardized and open to competitive bidding; foundry cost inflation at the specialized high-voltage BCD process nodes that MPS depends on; or customer ASP pressure if hyperscaler procurement teams begin leveraging MPS's growing revenue concentration against it in contract negotiations.

## The FY2024 Earnings Anomaly

The income statement for fiscal year 2024 contains a number that demands direct explanation. GAAP net income of $1.592 billion against GAAP operating income of $539 million is arithmetically impossible under a normal tax regime — the implied below-the-line item exceeds $1 billion. The explanation is a non-recurring deferred tax benefit that produced an effective tax rate of approximately negative 178% for the fiscal year. The precise mechanism — likely a release of valuation allowances on deferred tax assets as sustained profitability made future utilization probable, possibly combined with recognition of tax benefits related to equity compensation — produced a one-time GAAP earnings figure that inflated diluted EPS to $32.60 for FY2024 from $8.76 the prior year.

Analysts and investors were correct to strip this out. The normalized baseline for earnings analysis is FY2025 GAAP net income of $621 million on $2.79 billion in revenue, implying a net margin of approximately 22% and diluted EPS of $12.86. That is the run-rate earnings power of the business absent one-time accounting events — and it is the number against which the company's trailing P/E of approximately 120 (as of late May 2026) should be measured.

## Capital Allocation: The Discipline Behind the Growth

MPS's capital allocation framework reflects a clear hierarchy: invest aggressively in R&D, maintain a fortress balance sheet with zero financial debt, return growing cash to shareholders through dividends and selective buybacks, and grow organically rather than through acquisitions.

R&D spending has scaled from $191 million in FY2021 to $382 million in FY2025, representing approximately 13.7% of revenue — above the analog IC sector median of 10–12%. That investment rate is not a function of inefficiency; revenue per R&D dollar improved from approximately $6.30 in FY2021 to $7.30 in FY2025 as the product portfolio increasingly addresses higher-value power delivery problems. The R&D program is investing ahead of at least two product cycles simultaneously: wide-bandgap device drivers for SiC and GaN power stages targeting EV inverters and fast chargers, and next-generation digital controller firmware for AI accelerator platforms anticipated to exceed 1,500 watts per socket as NVIDIA's Vera Rubin and successor architectures arrive.

The balance sheet as of December 31, 2025 reported total stockholders' equity of $3.53 billion, retained earnings of $2.61 billion, and total liabilities of just $662.7 million — with zero long-term financial debt. MPS has operated debt-free throughout its public life. This is not a constraint imposed by capital market conditions; it is a deliberate posture. A fabless company with a large deferred tax asset base, deep retained earnings, and no capital-intensive manufacturing assets has no productive use for leverage, and the founders appear to view a clean balance sheet as strategic optionality rather than financial conservatism. The absence of debt also insulates MPS from interest rate exposure that has complicated the capital structure of some analog peers carrying acquisition-related leverage.

The dividend program has become an increasingly meaningful signal of management's confidence in free cash flow durability. In February 2026, concurrent with the Q4 2025 earnings release, the board increased the quarterly cash dividend 28% to $2.00 per share. At a quarterly rate that implies an annual payout of $8.00 per share, the dividend yield at current prices is modest — well under 1% of the stock price — but the growth rate of the payout is meaningful. A 28% increase is not the action of a management team hedging its growth outlook.

On acquisitions, MPS has been conspicuously absent from the M&A activity that characterized analog semiconductor consolidation — Analog Devices absorbing Linear Technology, Maxim Integrated, and Hittite; Texas Instruments building through acquisitions; Infineon purchasing Cypress and International Rectifier. Michael Hsing has consistently communicated a preference for organic development, citing the difficulty of integrating design cultures and process technologies. Whether that posture changes as the company approaches $3 billion in revenue and sits on a balance sheet capable of funding a multi-billion acquisition remains an open question; through the frozen snapshot date, it had not.

## The Forward View: Toward $3.5 Billion

Q1 2026 revenue of $804.2 million came in approximately $23 million above the sell-side consensus, extending the year-over-year growth rate to 26.1% — the same rate as full-year FY2025. GAAP operating margin reached 30.0%, a notable step-up from the 26.1% full-year FY2025 figure, suggesting operating leverage is beginning to manifest as enterprise data revenue scales against a largely fixed cost base.

Q2 2026 guidance of $890–910 million implies sequential growth of approximately 12% and year-over-year growth of approximately 43% at the midpoint — an acceleration from Q1's 26% that reflects both enterprise data ramp cadence and the order backlog management described as extending "well into Q3." Combining Q1 actuals of $804 million with the Q2 midpoint of $900 million yields first-half 2026 revenue of approximately $1.70 billion.

Extrapolating from CFO Bernie Blegen's guidance of "at least 50% growth" in enterprise data for the full year, and assuming Storage & Computing and Automotive hold their FY2025 growth trajectories at modestly lower rates given larger bases, a full-year FY2026 revenue range of $3.4–3.6 billion is arithmetically consistent with published guidance. That range embeds H2 2026 assumptions of $1.70–1.90 billion — roughly matching H1 or a modest step-up, with H2 dependent on Vera Rubin production ramp timing and hyperscaler capex execution remaining on current trajectories. The company has not provided explicit FY2026 annual guidance, but management's segment-level commentary leaves little ambiguity about the direction.

chapters.title: Pricing Perfection: Valuation Multiples, Peer Comparisons, and the Bull / Base / Bear Framework at $79 Billion
chapters.body:
## The Starting Multiple and Its Distortions

On May 23, 2026, Monolithic Power Systems closed at approximately $1,616 per share, a price that placed the San Jose company's market capitalisation at $79.4 billion. The headline statistic most analysts reached for first — a trailing price-to-earnings multiple of roughly 120 times — demands immediate qualification before meaningful comparison is possible.

The trailing P/E rests on FY2025 GAAP diluted earnings per share of $12.86, which itself requires context against the anomalous year prior. FY2024 net income of $1.59 billion was inflated by a non-recurring deferred tax benefit — the effective tax rate ran at approximately negative 178 per cent — producing a diluted EPS of $32.60 that year. Any trailing metric incorporating FY2024 data must strip out that windfall. FY2025's $621 million in GAAP net income represents the normalised earnings base, and the 120× trailing multiple therefore reflects a genuinely elevated, rather than arithmetically distorted, entry point.

Even the $12.86 figure requires a second adjustment. MPS's GAAP earnings carry approximately $298 million in annual stock-based compensation, representing roughly eleven per cent of FY2025 revenue. Excluding that non-cash charge — as most technology-sector investors do when constructing operating models — lifts normalised earnings by approximately $6 per share, reducing the effective trailing non-GAAP multiple to roughly 85 times. On a forward basis, with FY2026 non-GAAP EPS consensus estimates clustered around $22–$23 per share (anchored by Q1 2026's $5.10 quarterly non-GAAP result and a Q2 guidance midpoint of $900 million), the forward non-GAAP P/E compresses to approximately 70–75 times. That is still a historically elevated multiple for any component supplier, but the relevant comparison set is not the analog sector median.

## Peer Comparisons: The Premium and Its Justification

A clean reading of how MPS's valuation compares with the five closest analog and power semiconductor peers begins with the table below. Figures represent approximate consensus estimates as of the frozen snapshot date.

| Company | Ticker | Fwd P/E | EV/EBITDA | EV/Sales | 3-yr Rev CAGR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **MPS** | MPWR | ~72× | ~85× | ~22× | ~16% |
| Texas Instruments | TXN | ~28× | ~19× | ~11× | ~(1)% |
| Analog Devices | ADI | ~33× | ~24× | ~13× | ~(4)% |
| Renesas Electronics | 6723.T | ~14× | ~9× | ~3× | ~9% |
| Infineon Technologies | IFX.DE | ~19× | ~11× | ~2.5× | ~8% |
| ON Semiconductor | ON | ~15× | ~9× | ~2.5× | ~14% |

*Approximate consensus estimates, May 2026. MPS multiples derived from company financials and Q2 2026 guidance. Peer multiples reflect analyst consensus and available filings.*

Several observations emerge. MPS trades at a multiple two to four times its closest analog peer on virtually every metric — 72× forward P/E versus TXN's 28× and ADI's 33×, and 22× EV/Sales against a peer median closer to 4–5×. The three-year revenue CAGR differential partially but not fully explains the premium: MPS's 16% trailing CAGR (FY2022–FY2025) is itself the product of a flat FY2023 followed by accelerating FY2024 and FY2025 gains; running the same calculation from FY2023 to FY2025 produces 24%. Texas Instruments and Analog Devices, both working through multi-year inventory corrections stemming from the 2022–2023 supply chain normalisation cycle, posted negative compounded growth over the same period. ON Semiconductor, the nearest growth peer at roughly 14% CAGR, trades at a 15× forward P/E — a fraction of MPS's multiple — because its growth vector is silicon carbide power devices, a commodity market, rather than a CPU and GPU voltage-regulator franchise with locked-in hyperscaler qualification cycles. The real premium driver is the AI data centre optionality embedded in MPS's FY2026 and FY2027 enterprise data trajectory. Markets are pricing MPS not as an analog IC company but as a critical-path supplier to the most capital-intensive technology cycle in a decade.

## Historical Multiple Context

Three years of MPS trading history bracket the current multiple usefully. At the peak of AI infrastructure enthusiasm in late 2023 and early 2024, the stock commanded forward P/E multiples approaching 65–70× on then-current non-GAAP estimates — a premium that corrected sharply in mid-2025 when supply-chain concerns pushed the stock to a 52-week low near $392, implying a trough forward P/E of approximately 35–40 times. The current reading of roughly 72× forward non-GAAP sits above the three-year median but below the mid-2024 euphoria peak when Vera Rubin optimism first entered consensus models.

On the EV/Sales dimension, the stock reached approximately 25–28× trailing sales during the FY2024 AI run, troughed near 10–12× during the 2023 inventory correction, and now sits at approximately 22× on FY2026 estimates. That places current EV/Sales at the upper end of the three-year range without breaching the absolute peak — a configuration that limits near-term multiple expansion and puts clean execution squarely in the driver's seat.

## Three Scenarios: Bull, Base, and Bear

**Bull case.** Enterprise data segment revenue grows 70 per cent in FY2026, from $702 million to roughly $1.19 billion, as Vera Rubin content ramps at maximum analyst estimates — approximately 70 per cent of power management silicon per GPU tray — and hyperscaler customers pull inventory forward. Automotive sustains 40 per cent growth on 48V architecture proliferation and Chinese EV content wins, lifting the segment to approximately $830 million. Total FY2026 revenue approaches $3.75 billion. At 56 per cent gross margins and 38 per cent non-GAAP operating margins, non-GAAP operating income approaches $1.43 billion; after a 15 per cent effective tax rate and approximately 48 million diluted shares, non-GAAP EPS lands near $25.50. Applying a 75× premium multiple — justified if Vera Rubin ramp confirms MPS as the dominant GPU power supplier for the next platform generation — implies a price target range of **$1,900–$2,000**, approximately 20 per cent above the frozen snapshot price.

**Base case.** The enterprise data floor of "at least 50 per cent" growth as guided by management materialises: the segment reaches approximately $1.05 billion. Automotive delivers 30 per cent growth to $770 million. Storage and Computing grows 15 per cent to $842 million. Communications and industrial contribute modest single-digit to low-double-digit gains. Total FY2026 revenue settles near $3.5 billion. At 55 per cent gross margins and 36 per cent non-GAAP operating margins, non-GAAP EPS prints approximately $22. A multiple commensurate with a company growing at 25 per cent with expanding margins and proven AI-platform share might be 65–68×, implying a base case target range of **$1,430–$1,500** — essentially in line with current prices. The stock therefore prices in base-case execution with precision, offering limited upside unless the bull scenario materialises.

**Bear case.** AI capex sentiment reverses in the second half of 2026. A Vera Rubin ramp delay — whether from TSMC advanced packaging constraints or hyperscaler spend reallocation — reduces MPS's enterprise data growth to 30 per cent, well below the management floor. Simultaneously, commodity VR controller pricing intensifies as Asian competitors close the multi-phase controller specification gap. Gross margins compress 150–200 basis points to 53–53.5 per cent. Total FY2026 revenue falls short at approximately $3.1 billion. Non-GAAP EPS drops to approximately $18.50 as operating deleverage bites. At multiple compression to 45–50 times — consistent with what a decelerating AI-linked supplier would command in a risk-off environment — the implied price range falls to **$830–$925**, a 40–45 per cent drawdown from the frozen snapshot price.

## What the Market Has Priced In

At $79.4 billion against implied FY2026 revenue of approximately $3.5 billion, the market assigns roughly 22× EV/Sales. Unpacking that figure through a simplified framework: a company generating 55 per cent gross margins, expanding non-GAAP operating margins toward 37–38 per cent, and growing at 25 per cent annually would, at steady state five years forward, produce approximately $1.5–$1.8 billion in annual free cash flow. Discounted at a 9 per cent cost of equity with a 5 per cent terminal growth assumption, the present value arrives at approximately $60–$70 billion — below current trading but achievable under a bull trajectory. The 22× EV/Sales multiple therefore embeds continuation of the AI capex supercycle, gross margin defence, and operating leverage delivering on the upper end of non-GAAP targets. Any meaningful degradation in any of those three assumptions triggers valuation arithmetic that is uncomfortable.

## The DCF Trap Door

Monolithic Power's balance sheet provides a degree of financial resilience that most growth-premium names lack: zero long-term debt, $3.53 billion in stockholders' equity, and a growing dividend raised 28 per cent to $2.00 per share quarterly in early 2026. The fabless model keeps capital expenditure structurally low — typically two to four per cent of revenue versus twenty to thirty per cent for integrated device manufacturers — which amplifies free cash flow conversion from operating income. In a discounted cash flow model, these characteristics support a modestly lower discount rate assumption, perhaps 8.5 per cent rather than the 9.5–10 per cent applied to more leveraged names.

The problem is sensitivity. At a 120× trailing GAAP P/E starting point, the DCF is acutely exposed to terminal growth rate and discount rate assumptions. A 100-basis-point increase in the weighted average cost of capital — from 9 per cent to 10 per cent — reduces intrinsic value by roughly 20–25 per cent. A terminal growth rate assumption of 4 per cent rather than 5 per cent has a similarly deflating effect. For a company priced as a long-duration compounder, the gap between "AI capex sustains and rates remain contained" and "growth decelerates or rates rise" is not incremental — it is the arithmetic distance between the bull and bear scenarios laid out above. Investors who own MPS at $79 billion are not making a measured margin-of-safety bet. They are making a high-conviction wager on the duration of the AI infrastructure supercycle, on NVIDIA's continued platform dominance, and on Michael Hsing's ability to hold design-win share through Vera Rubin and whatever GPU generation follows it.

chapters.title: The Quarterly Cadence: Management Commentary, Demand Signals, and the AI-Driven Seasonality Reset
chapters.body:
## The Revenue Staircase: Five Quarters of Compounding Momentum

The quarterly earnings cadence at Monolithic Power Systems told a remarkably consistent story across the twelve months ended December 31, 2025: a company that had discovered a structural demand accelerant in AI infrastructure and was scaling into it quarter by quarter with almost metronomic regularity. Revenue in Q1 2025 stood at $637.6 million — respectable growth for a semiconductor company navigating post-inventory-correction headwinds, but not yet the number that would reframe how the market thought about MPS's positioning. Q2 2025 delivered $664.6 million, a modest sequential gain that reflected the early ramp of enterprise data wins alongside steady contributions from automotive and storage and computing. By Q3 2025, the acceleration was unmistakable: $737.2 million, up 11 percent sequentially, as hyperscaler procurement cycles aligned with MPS's Blackwell-generation power delivery shipments. Q4 2025 closed at $751.2 million — a then-record quarterly figure representing 20.8 percent year-over-year growth — capping a full-year 2025 result of $2.79 billion, up 26.4 percent from the prior year.

| Quarter | Revenue | Sequential Change | YoY Change |
|---------|---------|-------------------|------------|
| Q1 2025 | $637.6M | — | — |
| Q2 2025 | $664.6M | +4.2% | — |
| Q3 2025 | $737.2M | +11.0% | — |
| Q4 2025 | $751.2M | +1.9% | +20.8% |
| Q1 2026 | $804.2M | +7.1% | +26.1% |

Each sequential gain carried its own narrative weight. The Q3 step-up reflected the first full-quarter contribution from Blackwell program ramps and an automotive segment that had grown 43 percent for the full year. The modest Q4 sequential gain of 1.9 percent — below what investors had come to expect in what is typically MPS's strongest seasonal quarter — created momentary anxiety on the buy side: was demand decelerating, or was the supply chain absorbing inventory? Management's answer, delivered on the February 2026 earnings call, proved definitive.

## The Seasonality Inversion

For most of MPS's history, Q1 was the company's softest quarter. Consumer electronics demand fell away after the holiday sell-through cycle, notebook ODMs paused replenishment, and automotive customers managed inventory into model-year transitions. The seasonal pattern was well understood by sell-side analysts and priced into consensus expectations accordingly — Q1 was where you absorbed the year's lowest revenue and lowest gross margin utilization before the industrial and computing recovery began in Q2.

Q1 2026 broke that pattern decisively. Revenue of $804.2 million represented a 7.1 percent sequential increase over Q4 2025's record — the opposite of the typical Q1 trough — and a 26.1 percent year-over-year gain. The result beat consensus estimates of approximately $781.6 million by roughly $22 million, or 2.8 percent, a beat-magnitude that in the context of MPS's scale was meaningful. Enterprise Data and Communications were the proximate drivers: Enterprise Data was said to have grown nearly 100 percent year-over-year in the quarter, while Communications grew more than 50 percent.

The structural explanation was straightforward, even if its magnitude was surprising. Hyperscaler capital expenditure cycles — the procurement rhythms of Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, and Amazon Web Services — do not follow consumer electronics seasonality. Data center buildout is a multi-year capital program driven by enterprise planning cycles, GPU allocation commitments, and power infrastructure lead times, not by holiday sell-through or back-to-school demand. Once MPS had established a significant revenue base in enterprise data — approximately $702 million in FY2025, roughly 25 percent of total revenue — the consumer-driven seasonal trough in Q1 was no longer capable of pulling the consolidated revenue line downward. The AI infrastructure capex cycle had, in effect, provided a permanent revenue floor that consumer seasonality could no longer pierce.

The GAAP operating margin trajectory reinforced this interpretation. Q1 2026's 30.0 percent GAAP operating margin was a step-function above the full-year FY2025 level of 26.1 percent, and the non-GAAP operating margin reached 35.8 percent. Operating leverage was beginning to compound as enterprise data revenue — which carries structurally high gross margins given the proprietary BCD process and module integration content — scaled to a larger share of the mix.

## Backlog, Book-to-Bill, and the Visibility Signal

The Q4 2025 earnings call in February 2026 introduced a data point that resonated through analyst models for weeks afterward: management characterized the book-to-bill ratio as well above 1.0, with backlog extending meaningfully into Q2 and Q3 2026. In a sector that had spent 2023 and early 2024 digesting bloated customer inventories accumulated during the pandemic supply-chain panic, a book-to-bill comfortably above parity carried genuine signal value.

The backlog commentary served multiple functions. It indicated that hyperscaler customers were not front-loading orders as an inventory buffer hedge — a behavior that had led to the 2022–2023 correction cycle across the broader semiconductor industry — but were instead placing orders aligned with actual rack deployment timelines. MPS's enterprise data ASPs had stabilized, and the absence of price concession pressure in the backlog suggested that customers viewed MPS's power delivery content as relatively inelastic: the engineering qualification friction and design-win lock-in economics of a multi-phase digital controller in a GPU reference design afforded MPS pricing stability that commodity analog suppliers could not replicate.

CFO Bernie Blegen, who had served as MPS's primary financial voice on earnings calls for over a decade, delivered the revised guidance on that February call with characteristic precision:

> "We are raising our enterprise data growth floor for 2026 to at least 50 percent, based on improving backlog visibility, new program ramps, and a broadening of our hyperscaler customer base beyond a single anchor relationship."

That single phrase — "at least 50 percent" on an enterprise data base of approximately $702 million — implied greater than $1 billion in enterprise data revenue for FY2026. For a segment that had contributed approximately $148 million in FY2023, the two-year compounding rate embedded in that floor was, by any analog semiconductor historical standard, extraordinary.

## The CFO Transition: Signal or Noise?

Blegen's retirement following the issuance of the 2025 Form 10-K introduced a variable that investor relations observers tracked closely. Long-tenured CFOs are bearers of institutional communication style — the cadence of guidance conservatism, the vocabulary of margin framing, the precision of segment-level commentary. Corporate Controller Rob Dean, appointed interim CFO, had served in that capacity for nine years and was deeply familiar with MPS's financial architecture. But familiarity with the books is distinct from the muscle memory of managing quarterly earnings communication under investor scrutiny.

The Q1 2026 results suggested the transition introduced minimal friction. Guidance for Q2 2026 — $890 to $910 million in revenue, with GAAP gross margin of 55.1 to 55.7 percent — was delivered with a specificity and forward-conviction that matched the prior regime's communication standard. The midpoint of $900 million implied 43 percent year-over-year growth and a sequential acceleration of roughly 12 percent, consistent with the backlog signals from February. If Dean adopted any change from Blegen's approach, it was perhaps a marginally tighter guidance band — a $20 million range versus the $25–30 million bands occasionally used in prior years — which read as confidence rather than caution.

## The Q2 2026 Setup: Execution Requirements and Downside Topology

Q2 2026 guidance of $890–910 million sets a demanding bar. Reaching the high end of that range — approximately $910 million — would require Enterprise Data to sustain its near-doubling pace, Automotive to continue its mid-to-high single-digit sequential cadence as Chinese EV volumes and ADAS domain controller ramps contributed, and Storage and Computing to hold its recovery trajectory as AI-adjacent accelerator memory sockets expanded.

The high-end scenario was not a stretch case under the backlog conditions management described. MPS's Vera Rubin design wins — with analyst estimates placing MPS content at approximately 70 percent of addressable power management silicon per GPU tray — represented a product-cycle step-up in ASP and volume beyond the Blackwell baseline. If Vera Rubin rack deployments accelerated through Q2 and Q3 2026 as hyperscaler procurement teams indicated, the high end of guidance carried upside optionality rather than risk.

The downside scenario, by contrast, was concentrated and binary. A slip in NVIDIA's Vera Rubin production timeline, a hyperscaler capex pause driven by AI return-on-investment concerns, or an inventory build at ODM partners in advance of platform transitions could compress enterprise data revenue against a quarterly comparison that now demanded continuation of a near-100 percent year-over-year growth rate. At a trailing P/E of approximately 120 and a stock that had moved from near $392 to a 52-week high approaching $1,798, the market had priced in sustained execution. A miss of even 3–4 percent against the midpoint of Q2 guidance would not simply reset quarterly expectations — it would trigger a reassessment of the structural AI narrative itself.

The quarterly cadence, having delivered five consecutive quarters of acceleration, had now set a floor from which any deviation carried asymmetric consequences. That was both the promise and the burden of MPS's position at the center of the AI power delivery stack.

chapters.title: The Founder's Machine: Michael Hsing, the CFO Transition, and the Governance Questions at $79 Billion Scale
chapters.body:
## The Founder's Fingerprints

Michael Hsing did not arrive at chief executive by way of a finance rotation or a series of operational promotions. He arrived by way of a laboratory. Before founding Monolithic Power Systems on August 22, 1997, Hsing had spent the preceding years at Supertex and Micrel Semiconductor — two Silicon Valley analog houses where he worked as a senior silicon process developer, accumulating deep expertise in high-voltage bipolar-CMOS-DMOS integration. His academic formation was similarly eclectic: a bachelor's degree in Foreign Languages and Literature from National Taiwan University, followed by a master's in Computer Science from the New York Institute of Technology. He is, in the precise meaning of the term, a process engineer who founded a public company and never stopped being one.

That biographical trajectory has shaped Monolithic Power Systems at every level. The company's foundational competitive advantage — its proprietary BCD process platform, which integrates high-voltage power stages, precision analog control loops, and digital interfaces on a single die — is not a licensing position or an acquired capability. It is the direct expression of Hsing's technical thesis, formulated in the mid-1990s, that monolithic integration could displace the discrete power circuitry then ubiquitous in notebook and consumer OEM designs. Twenty-eight years later, Hsing still speaks about product architecture in granular detail in public forums. On the Q4 2025 earnings call, he characterized MPS's positioning on NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform not in revenue terms but in systems-level terms — describing the power delivery architecture, the multi-phase controller topology, and the module integration strategy before his finance team addressed the financial metrics. That sequencing is not an accident.

## The CFO Succession: A Governance Gap at an Inflection Point

The retirement of Bernie Blegen following the issuance of MPS's FY2025 Form 10-K was, on the surface, an orderly transition. Blegen had served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer for roughly fifteen years, a tenure that spanned MPS's inclusion in the S&P 500, its pivot from consumer electronics supplier to AI infrastructure vendor, and its revenue scaling from approximately $300 million to $2.79 billion. In each of those years, Blegen provided capital markets continuity that a founder-CEO with deep engineering immersion but limited public markets instinct might not have delivered alone. His communication style on earnings calls was measured, precise, and credible to institutional investors.

His successor is not, as of the snapshot date, a successor in the full sense. Rob Dean, the company's nine-year Corporate Controller, was appointed interim CFO. Dean's institutional knowledge of MPS's accounting systems, cost structure, and reporting cadence is genuine — nine years as controller of a high-growth semiconductor company provides a substantive operational foundation. But the interim designation matters. MPS entered fiscal 2026 with enterprise data revenue growing at a floor of 50% year-over-year, Q2 2026 guidance of $890–$910 million implying 43% annual growth, and a book-to-bill ratio described by management as "well above 1.0." This is not a company that is consolidating. It is a company that is compressing multiple growth phases into a narrow window and requires capital markets dialogue that reaches beyond internal continuity.

As of the snapshot date, MPS had made no public disclosure of a permanent CFO search timeline. Sell-side analysts flagged the gap as a modest governance concern — modest because Dean handled his initial earnings appearances competently, and modest because Blegen's departure was planned rather than abrupt. But the absence of a search announcement, in a period when MPS is arguably more visible to institutional investors than at any prior point in its history, raises a reasonable question about whether the board moved with sufficient urgency.

## Herbert Chang and the Independence Calculus

Herbert Chang joined the MPS board in September 1999, five years before the company's 2004 IPO. He has held the Lead Independent Director title and presides over executive sessions of independent directors. His day job, since 2014, has been General Manager of Mutto Optronics Corporation, a Taiwan OTC-listed manufacturer of optical lenses and knife blades.

The gap between Mutto Optronics and a $79 billion market-capitalization AI infrastructure semiconductor company is not subtle. Chang's value to the board lies not in domain expertise but in institutional memory: he was present for Hsing's original product theses, the early customer negotiations, the IPO, and the successive strategic pivots. In a company that has moved this quickly, that memory has real worth. But it is not the same as independent oversight, and the proxy advisory community has a clear framework for evaluating the question.

Under [ISS](https://www.issgovernance.com) and Glass Lewis tenure guidelines, independent directors with more than approximately nine to twelve years of service begin to attract scrutiny regarding their effective independence from management. Chang's 26-year tenure on the board — and his appointment to the Lead Independent Director role — sits well outside that range. The 2025 DEF 14A, filed in April 2025, contains the board's formal independence assessment: it determined that Chang qualified as independent under NASDAQ listing standards and SEC rules. That determination reflects legal threshold compliance, not governance best practice. The structural tension between Chang's institutional intimacy with Hsing and the formal independence requirement of the Lead Independent Director role is a latent governance risk that institutional proxy advisors are positioned to surface at any future shareholder vote where dilution, succession, or related-party transactions are on the agenda.

## Carintia Martinez: Relevant Expertise, Potential Disclosure Complexity

Carintia Martinez joined the MPS board in May 2021 and chairs the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. Her credentials are the most directly relevant to MPS's fastest-growing legacy vertical: a decade-plus at Renault Group in digital transformation and IT leadership roles, followed by a VP and CIO position at Thales Alenia Space, and then CIO tenures at IHS Towers and, since February 2025, Chief Digital Information Officer of Automotive Cells Company.

ACC is not a peripheral entity. It is the EV battery joint venture formed by Stellantis, TotalEnergies, and Mercedes-Benz — a Tier 1 EV supply chain actor in the European automotive ecosystem. MPS's automotive segment generated $592.5 million in FY2025 revenue, representing 21% of the company's total, and the company supplies power management ICs to Tier 1 automotive suppliers including Continental, Aptiv, Bosch, and Valeo, as well as to several Chinese EV OEMs directly.

The question this creates is disclosure completeness rather than a straightforward conflict. Martinez is a technology and digital transformation executive at ACC, not a procurement or supply chain decision-maker. Her role does not, on its face, create a direct transactional conflict with MPS's automotive IC supply relationships. But ACC participates in EV supply chains that MPS's customers and prospective customers inhabit, and the 2025 proxy materials should address — and investors should verify — whether any conflict-of-interest disclosure was filed at the time of ACC's appointment to her role in February 2025, and whether that disclosure was updated in the subsequent proxy. Martinez's appointment to the governance committee chairmanship, which oversees director independence determinations, makes this disclosure hygiene material rather than theoretical.

## Compensation Architecture and Shareholder Alignment

The April 2025 DEF 14A proxy provides the formal record of Hsing's compensation structure. As founder-Chairman-President-CEO — a four-role concentration unusual even by founder-led semiconductor standards — Hsing's total reported compensation includes a cash salary component, an annual cash incentive award, and a large equity grant structured as performance-based restricted stock units. The Compensation Committee weights non-GAAP metrics heavily in the annual incentive plan, including non-GAAP earnings per share and non-GAAP operating income — metrics that exclude stock-based compensation expense, acquisition-related amortization, and certain other items.

This weighting matters at MPS's scale because stock-based compensation is not a trivial line item. A company that relies significantly on equity compensation to attract and retain engineering talent — particularly in the competitive AI semiconductor labor market — creates shareholder dilution that GAAP-based metrics capture and non-GAAP metrics obscure. Compensation committee performance metrics that favor non-GAAP outcomes structurally align management incentives toward reported cash profitability rather than capital efficiency on a fully diluted basis. As MPS approaches the $3–4 billion revenue range, institutional investors with long-only mandates increasingly scrutinize this structure.

## The Governance Assessment: Scale Has Outrun Structure

MPS will, under its own guidance trajectory and sell-side consensus, approach $3.5–4 billion in annual revenue within two to three years. It operates a largest-globally R&D center in Chengdu, Sichuan, employing more than 2,800 staff across China. Its primary growth engine is entangled with NVIDIA's GPU roadmap, a customer-concentration dynamic that has been partially but not fully mitigated by hyperscaler diversification. Its second-largest segment is automotive, a geopolitically complex supply chain that spans European JVs, Chinese OEM direct relationships, and U.S. ADAS content.

Against that operational backdrop, the current board composition — a founder-Chairman who is simultaneously the company's most important technical decision-maker, a 26-year Lead Independent Director with no semiconductor domain expertise, and one genuinely relevant independent director appointed in 2021 — reflects the governance structure of a mid-cap specialist, not the oversight architecture appropriate to a near-$80 billion market capitalization AI infrastructure company. The absence of a permanent CFO, the lack of a disclosed succession framework for Hsing himself, and the tenure question surrounding Chang are not individually catastrophic governance failures. Collectively, they represent a structural lag between the pace at which the business has scaled and the pace at which its governance apparatus has evolved to match. For a company that has compounded shareholder value at a rate its founder can credibly attribute to his own technical vision, that lag has carried limited cost to date. As MPS moves deeper into geopolitically sensitive supply chains and grows its dependence on a single flagship customer architecture, the cost of governance inertia rises.

chapters.title: The Customer Constellation: NVIDIA, Hyperscalers, Automotive Tier 1s, and the Six-Segment Revenue Architecture
chapters.body:
By the close of FY2025, Monolithic Power Systems had constructed a revenue architecture that bore little resemblance to the notebook power-rail specialist Michael Hsing founded in 1997. The company's $2.79 billion in annual revenue spanned six end markets, anchored at its apex by a relationship with NVIDIA that had evolved from peripheral supplier to critical infrastructure partner over the course of a single GPU generation — and was poised to deepen further with the Vera Rubin architecture then ramping into production.

## The NVIDIA Relationship: From Design-Win to Critical Path

MPS's insertion into NVIDIA's supply chain deepened progressively with each successive architecture. The H100 generation established MPS as a qualified multi-phase controller supplier; the Blackwell family — encompassing the GB100 and GB200 — elevated that position to include complete integrated power modules. The MP2891 dual-loop eight-phase controller emerged as a reference design component for high-density GPU server trays, where peak power delivery requirements exceeded 1,000 watts per socket.

The Vera Rubin architecture, NVIDIA's next-generation GPU platform expected to ramp through 2026 and 2027, has drawn the most sustained analyst attention in MPS's investment narrative. Multiple sell-side reports published in early-to-mid 2026 estimated MPS's content capture at approximately 70 percent of addressable power management silicon per Vera Rubin GPU tray — a figure that, if accurate, would represent a step-function increase relative to the Blackwell-era position. MPS has not publicly confirmed a specific content share; the company's standard disclosure practice reports segment-level revenue without naming OEM customers or their contribution to a given segment. The 70 percent estimate derives from analyst teardowns of Blackwell reference designs, extrapolated forward on the assumption that MPS's design-win incumbency has not been disrupted by competitive re-qualification.

That assumption rests on structural logic: power delivery design wins in GPU architectures are inherently sticky. Once an MPS controller is qualified into an NVIDIA reference platform, it is replicated across the full manufacturing run — potentially tens of millions of trays built by Foxconn, Quanta, Wistron, and Inventec. Displacing a qualified power architecture mid-generation carries qualification cost and schedule risk that ODMs and system integrators are unwilling to absorb.

## The Six-Segment Architecture

[FY2025 revenue](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001280452/000143774926006113/mpwr20251231_10k.htm) of $2.79 billion broke down as follows:

| Segment | FY2025 Revenue | YoY Growth | Share of Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Storage & Computing | $732.5M | +46% | 26% |
| Enterprise Data | ~$702M | 2yr CAGR >100% | 25% |
| Automotive | $592.5M | +43% | 21% |
| Communications | ~$309M | — | 11% |
| Consumer | ~$255M | — | 9% |
| Industrial | ~$199M | — | 7% |

The two fastest-growing segments — Enterprise Data and Storage & Computing — together accounted for 51 percent of total FY2025 revenue, reflecting the structural rotation of MPS's revenue mix toward AI infrastructure and the compute substrate that supports it.

## Enterprise Data: The Hyperscaler-NVIDIA Complex

Enterprise Data, at roughly $702 million, had grown from approximately $148 million in FY2023 over two years — a cumulative expansion exceeding 375 percent. The segment encompasses power management ICs for AI accelerator trays, cloud server racks, and associated networking infrastructure.

The procurement channel is bifurcated. NVIDIA-specific design wins flow through the ODM supply chain: hyperscalers such as Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, and Amazon Web Services specify GPU server configurations; NVIDIA qualifies reference designs; ODMs — principally Foxconn Industrial Internet, Quanta Computer, Wistron, and Inventec — build to those specifications and procure MPS components at the bill-of-materials level. MPS therefore recognizes revenue against ODMs rather than directly against hyperscalers in most GPU tray configurations. This creates revenue timing complexity: MPS shipments track ODM production schedules, which in turn track hyperscaler purchase orders, which reflect capital expenditure commitments made quarters in advance. A second, more direct channel exists for custom AI silicon platforms; hyperscalers with proprietary accelerator designs may embed MPS controllers directly into their custom silicon reference boards through direct procurement.

On the Q4 2025 earnings call, outgoing CFO Bernie Blegen raised the enterprise data growth outlook:

> "At least 50 percent [growth in Enterprise Data for FY2026]."

Blegen attributed the upward revision to backlog visibility extending into Q3 2026 and deliberate diversification of the hyperscaler customer base beyond a single anchor program. At that floor, Enterprise Data revenue would exceed $1 billion in FY2026.

## Storage and Computing: The Revenue Leader

Storage and Computing, at $732.5 million (+46%), spans SSD controller power rails, DRAM module regulators, enterprise hard-disk drive electronics, notebook CPU and GPU voltage regulators, and discrete graphics card power stages. Named customer categories include Seagate, Western Digital, Micron, SK Hynix, Samsung, and the notebook ODM supply chains serving HP, Dell, and Lenovo.

The segment's growth in FY2025 was driven disproportionately by AI-infrastructure adjacency: enterprise SSD procurement for hyperscaler data centers accelerated alongside GPU server buildout, and high-bandwidth memory adoption — HBM3 in particular — created incremental power management sockets. MPS's multi-phase DRAM power controllers benefited from DDR5 and HBM3 adoption cycles, both of which require tighter voltage regulation tolerances than prior memory generations.

## Automotive: The Electrification Dividend
